chunks: What test points are and what they do. The question: What are test points? What are their use cases?
A test point is a small, labeled connection to a net on the board.
It is usually a pad, a loop of wire or a via (a small plated hole), placed there so a person or a machine can measure or drive that net.
Without test points you must probe the legs of parts, which is slow, risky and often impossible on modern small parts.
Think of the valve on a car tire. You do not cut into the tire to check the pressure. The valve is a deliberate access point, and anyone with a gauge can use it.
A test point is the same idea for a signal.
The analogy has one catch: a valve costs almost nothing, but a test point takes board space and adds a small load to the signal, so you place them where they matter.
One pad serves many customers over the product's life. The more customers a net has (power rails, resets, programming lines), the stronger the case for a test point.
Net: all the copper that is electrically one connection. Bring-up: the first power-on and debugging of a new board.
Bed-of-nails fixture: spring pins that touch many test points at once in factory testing. Ground reference: a nearby ground point; a test point is useless without one.
Stub: the short spur of copper that a test point adds to a signal.
A 1 mm round pad sitting 0. 1 mm above a ground plane adds about 0. 3 picofarads of capacitance, a tiny bit of charge storage that slows fast edges.
On a slow power supply line (a rail) that is nothing. On a signal running at multiple gigabits per second it can matter.
So power rails, ground, reset, clocks, programming lines and key analog nodes nearly always get test points, and the fastest nets get a tiny pad or none. That is the whole idea.
"A test point is a deliberate, labelled pad, loop or via on a net so something can measure or drive it.

Engineers use them during bring-up and debug to probe rails and signals, factories use them for in-circuit and functional test, programming and calibration, and technicians use them for diagnosis in the field.
They cost a little area and, on fast nets, some capacitance, so I place them on the nets where observability matters most."
